messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mei Tan was 51, a married dentist who had built a careful, orderly life in her practice and home, yet she arrived for treatment sounding as if the world had become difficult to trust. The trauma began three years earlier, when a man she had briefly met outside work started appearing again and again in places she had no reason to expect him. At first it was small enough to dismiss: a note left on her car, a familiar-looking vehicle slowing outside the clinic, a voice message that was unsettling but still deniable. Then the contact sharpened into stalking that reached into her routines, and Mei became aware that she was being watched, mapped, and anticipated. What unsettled her most was that it happened in ordinary, public settings, in daylight, in places where she had always assumed she would be protected by busyness and by other people. She described a growing conviction that if someone wanted access to her, they could find it.

Since then, certain songs have become impossible for Mei to hear without a jolt of dread. A tune that once played in her car radio, or in a waiting room, can pull her back into the period when she was checking mirrors, scanning sidewalks, and bracing for another message or another appearance. Related media content has the same effect: a news story, a drama scene, or even a passing reference to stalking can make her body go tense before she has fully registered what she is hearing. Police presence is no comfort to her in the way it seems to be for others. Seeing officers near her building or outside the clinic does not settle her; it reminds her that the situation had become serious enough to involve authority, and yet it also leaves her with the sense that danger can still be real right in front of everyone. Each of these moments seems to confirm what she fears most: even when others tell her she is safe, she finds it impossible to believe it.

Over time, Mei began arranging her life around where she could sit and what she could see. In the clinic lunchroom, in restaurants with her husband, in waiting areas between patients, she always chooses a seat based on how protected she feels, and she is most comfortable with her back against a wall where she can watch the room. She said this is not about preference but about necessity, because being able to see who is coming toward her is the only thing that keeps her from feeling cornered. At work, she has become noticeably less relaxed with unfamiliar visitors and more alert whenever she hears a song playing from the reception area or sees a report on a screen in the waiting room. These are not dramatic episodes to her; they are the everyday reminders that make her mind return to the same conclusion. The songs, the media, and the sight of police all press the same message on her: danger can reappear without warning, and she cannot rely on reassurance from other people to override that sense.

As the months passed, Mei’s world narrowed. She found herself arriving early to choose a chair before the office filled, and she sometimes delayed leaving her practice until the hallway was quiet enough that she would not have to pass too many people. Her husband tried to reassure her, telling her that the stalker was long gone and that she was watched over, but the words seemed to slide off her. She did not interpret his reassurance as wrong so much as incomplete; if anything, it made her feel more alone, because it highlighted how little other people seemed to understand the degree to which her body still acted as though the threat were nearby. She was embarrassed by how much planning went into something as simple as sitting down, but the embarrassment did not change the habit. Instead, it made her quieter, more inward, and more determined to control what she could.

By the time she sought help, Mei was exhausted by the constant vigilance and by the way ordinary sensory cues could collapse a good day into fear. A song on the radio while she was driving to the clinic, a news clip in the staff room, or the sight of officers near the entrance could leave her unable to shake the conviction that danger was close and that she would not be able to trust safety even when everyone around her insisted on it. What finally brought her in was the realization that she was no longer just avoiding reminders of the stalking; she was organizing her whole life around them. She wanted relief from the unrelenting alarm, but what she feared most was that if she let her guard down, she would once again miss the moment when someone appeared too close, too suddenly, and she would be trapped with no wall at her back and no way to feel certain she could protect herself.
